Paragraph: bandhur ātmātmanas tasya yenātmaivātmanā jitaḥ | anātmanas tu śatrutve vartetātmaiva śatru-vat || To those who have mastered the mind, the brain is the greatest friend. for those who have not succeeded, it’s the most formidable foe.
Situation/Problem_Faced: The internal conflict of emotional turmoil, self-sabotage, and lack of mental control, where an disciplined mind becomes an enemy to one's own well-being.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna emphasizes the absolute necessity of self-mastery and mind control (Atma-samyama), explaining that the mind acts as an ally or an adversary based on internal discipline.
Outcome/Resolution: Empowerment through self-regulation, transforming the mind from an internal source of conflict into an instrument of resilience, clarity, and peace.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Stress Management: Internal locus of control, Mental discipline

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Atma-samyama (Self-control and mastery over mind and senses)
Manas-Mitra vs. Manas-Satru (The mind as a friend or an enemy depending on self-discipline)
Samatvam (Inner balance and equilibrium through mental mastery)
Viveka (Discernment to guide the mind constructively)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: This verse from Dhyana Yoga establishes that the self is responsible for its own elevation or degradation. A subjugated, disciplined mind acts as a spiritual ally, whereas an uncontrolled mind behaves like an external enemy.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this highlights cognitive-behavioral self-regulation and neuroplasticity concepts. Uncontrolled intrusive thoughts and dysregulated emotions create internal distress, while developing self-mastery fosters resilience and healthy self-efficacy.
